Lab 1b: Where Election Data Comes From

84-355 Democracy’s Data | Week 1 — Election returns

Your name here

August 06, 2026

Before we start

On Tuesday you drew a map of the 2024 election from a file that was simply handed to you, and we named the four families of evidence this course runs on:

Family Made by Made how Weeks
Election returns nobody in particular counted, canvassed, certified — separately, by every county and state this week
The census one agency, on a legal schedule a constitutionally required count, plus a rolling survey 2, 12–15
Surveys pollsters and agencies asking a sample and weighting the answers 3, 10
Administrative records a bureaucracy, as a by-product filings and logs kept for some other purpose 5, 7

Today is the first family, and it is the strangest of the four. The other three have a producer you can name. Returns do not.

Here is the chain that produces an official presidential result. A voter marks a ballot in a precinct. The precinct’s count goes to a county clerk, who canvasses it. The county sends a certified return to the secretary of state, who canvasses again and certifies a statewide total, usually a few weeks after election day. Nobody in that chain publishes a tidy national file. There is no national election administrator in the United States, and therefore no official national returns file. Every dataset you have ever seen of American election results was assembled by somebody — a news organization, an academic project, a hobbyist — who went out and collected fifty-one separate things and stapled them together.

Today you will do the stapling yourself, and watch it fail in four different ways. Keep asking, as each failure appears, whether it is a returns problem or a problem any data would have. Some of what breaks today breaks because nobody is in charge — and that is specific to this family.

The same rules as last week: grey blocks are code chunks, run them with the green ▶ arrow or Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Enter, everything is base R, and work in order because later chunks depend on earlier ones.

Part 1: Four files, and a trap in the first one

The data/ folder has four files.

File Rows What it is
pres2024_counties.csv 3,160 2024 presidential votes by county
pres2020_counties.csv 3,152 the same, for 2020
census_counties.csv 3,144 the Census Bureau’s official list of counties
pres2024_states.csv 51 last week’s state file, unchanged

Start with the county returns:

cty <- read.csv("data/pres2024_counties.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
head(cty)
#>   state_name county_fips    county_name votes_dem votes_gop total_votes
#> 1    Alabama        1001 Autauga County      7439     20484       28190
#> 2    Alabama        1003 Baldwin County     24934     95798      121808
#> 3    Alabama        1005 Barbour County      4158      5606        9832
#> 4    Alabama        1007    Bibb County      1619      7572        9241
#> 5    Alabama        1009  Blount County      2576     25354       28115
#> 6    Alabama        1011 Bullock County      2983      1101        4106

Everything looks fine. It is not.

Look at county_fips. A FIPS code is the federal government’s unique identifier for a place: two digits for the state, three for the county. Autauga County, Alabama is 01001 — state 01, county 001. That is a label, like a phone number. It is not a quantity.

But read.csv() looks at a column of digits and decides it is a number:

class(cty$county_fips)
#> [1] "integer"
head(cty$county_fips)
#> [1] 1001 1003 1005 1007 1009 1011

The leading zero is gone. 01001 has become the number 1001. How much damage?

table(nchar(cty$county_fips))
#> 
#>    4    5 
#>  328 2832
short <- cty[nchar(cty$county_fips) == 4, ]
sort(unique(short$state_name))
#> [1] "Alabama"     "Alaska"      "Arizona"     "Arkansas"    "California" 
#> [6] "Colorado"    "Connecticut"

Pause and read that output. 328 of 3,160 rows are broken, and they are not random — they are exactly the seven states whose FIPS code begins with a zero. Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut. If you later try to match these against any other government file, none of them will match, and the failure will be silent.

This is the single most common bug in real election-data work. Fix it by telling read.csv() that the column is text, not a number:

cty <- read.csv("data/pres2024_counties.csv",
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                colClasses = c(county_fips = "character"))

table(nchar(cty$county_fips))
#> 
#>    5 
#> 3160
head(cty$county_fips)
#> [1] "01001" "01003" "01005" "01007" "01009" "01011"

colClasses takes a named vector: the name is the column, the value is the type you want. Now every code is five characters, as it should be.

Read the other three files the same careful way:

old <- read.csv("data/pres2020_counties.csv",
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                colClasses = c(county_fips = "character"))

cen <- read.csv("data/census_counties.csv",
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                colClasses = c(fips = "character"))

st  <- read.csv("data/pres2024_states.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dim(cty); dim(old); dim(cen); dim(st)
#> [1] 3160    6
#> [1] 3152    6
#> [1] 3144    4
#> [1] 51 10

One more thing to notice before we go on. Compare the two 2024 files:

head(cty[, c("state_name", "county_name", "votes_dem", "votes_gop")], 3)
#>   state_name    county_name votes_dem votes_gop
#> 1    Alabama Autauga County      7439     20484
#> 2    Alabama Baldwin County     24934     95798
#> 3    Alabama Barbour County      4158      5606
head(st[, c("state", "harris", "trump")], 3)
#>     state harris trump
#> 1 Alabama  34.10 64.57
#> 2  Alaska  41.41 54.54
#> 3 Arizona  46.70 52.20

The county file is counts of ballots. The state file is percentages. You cannot add a percentage to a count, and you cannot compare them until you convert one to the other. That sounds obvious written down; it is a genuine source of published errors.

Part 2: Adding the counties up

If the county file is right and the state file is right, then adding up a state’s counties should reproduce that state’s result. Let’s find out.

aggregate() is the base R tool for “add up this column, grouped by that column.” The formula reads left side, broken out by right side:

agg <- aggregate(cbind(votes_dem, votes_gop, total_votes) ~ state_name,
                 data = cty, FUN = sum)

nrow(agg)
#> [1] 51
head(agg)
#>   state_name votes_dem votes_gop total_votes
#> 1    Alabama    772412   1462616     2256352
#> 2     Alaska    139690    184407      324097
#> 3    Arizona   1582860   1770242     3389319
#> 4   Arkansas    396905    759241     1182676
#> 5 California   9276179   6081697    15862536
#> 6   Colorado   1728159   1377441     3190873

51 rows — 50 states and DC, which is what we want. Now convert counts to percentages so the two files speak the same language:

agg$harris_c <- round(100 * agg$votes_dem / agg$total_votes, 2)
agg$trump_c  <- round(100 * agg$votes_gop / agg$total_votes, 2)

The _c suffix is a reminder: these came from the counties.

Now join the two tables. merge() matches rows between two data frames using a shared column. Ours are named differently, so we say which is which:

cmp <- merge(agg, st, by.x = "state_name", by.y = "state")
nrow(cmp)
#> [1] 51

51 rows out, 51 rows in. The join worked. Now the moment of truth:

cmp$dh <- round(cmp$harris_c - cmp$harris, 2)
cmp$dt <- round(cmp$trump_c  - cmp$trump,  2)

sum(cmp$dh == 0 & cmp$dt == 0)
#> [1] 18

Eighteen states agree exactly. Thirty-three do not. Here are the worst:

worst <- cmp[order(-abs(cmp$dh)), ]
head(worst[, c("state_name", "harris", "harris_c", "dh",
               "trump", "trump_c", "dt")], 8)
#>       state_name harris harris_c   dh trump trump_c   dt
#> 2         Alaska  41.41    43.10 1.69 54.54   56.90 2.36
#> 33      New York  55.12    56.34 1.22 42.71   43.66 0.95
#> 46       Vermont  63.83    64.36 0.53 32.32   32.59 0.27
#> 21      Maryland  62.62    63.09 0.47 34.08   34.34 0.26
#> 14      Illinois  54.37    54.77 0.40 43.47   43.79 0.32
#> 48    Washington  57.20    57.60 0.40 39.00   39.27 0.27
#> 38        Oregon  55.27    55.64 0.37 40.97   41.25 0.28
#> 22 Massachusetts  61.22    61.58 0.36 36.02   36.23 0.21

A picture of all 51:

top <- cmp[order(-abs(cmp$dh)), ][1:15, ]
top <- top[order(abs(top$dh)), ]

par(mar = c(5, 10, 4, 2))
barplot(top$dh,
        names.arg = top$state_name,
        horiz = TRUE, las = 1, border = NA,
        col = ifelse(abs(top$dh) > 1, "#B2182B", "#999999"),
        xlim = c(0, 2),
        xlab = "County sum minus state file (Harris, percentage points)",
        main = "Where the two files disagree")

Pause and read that plot. Two things are strange. First, Alaska and New York are in a class of their own. Second — and this is the real clue — look at the direction. Check it:

c(higher = sum(cmp$dh > 0), equal = sum(cmp$dh == 0), lower = sum(cmp$dh < 0))
#> higher  equal  lower 
#>     32     19      0

Every single disagreement runs the same way. The county sums never give Harris a lower share than the state file; they give her a higher one, or the same one. Random errors do not behave like that. A one-sided error means something systematic, and systematic errors have findable causes.

Before we chase it: does any of this change who won?

cmp$winner_c <- ifelse(cmp$harris_c > cmp$trump_c, "Harris", "Trump")
sum(cmp$winner_c != cmp$winner)
#> [1] 0

No. Zero states flip. That is worth saying plainly, because it is the honest summary: the disagreement is real, it is systematic, and it does not change the outcome. All three parts of that sentence matter.

Part 3: The vote that isn’t there

If Harris’s share is too high in the county sums, either her count is too big or the denominator is too small. Let’s look at the denominator.

Every county’s total_votes should be Harris plus Trump plus everybody else. So everybody else is:

cty$other <- cty$total_votes - cty$votes_gop - cty$votes_dem
summary(cty$other)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#>      0.0     50.0    138.5    810.8    430.2 121456.0

No negatives, so the arithmetic is at least internally consistent. But look at the minimum. How many counties report zero third-party votes?

sum(cty$other == 0)
#> [1] 107

In 2024 more than two million people voted for someone other than Harris or Trump. In how many counties did literally nobody? Almost certainly none. So a zero here is not a measurement. Where are they?

zeros <- tapply(cty$other, cty$state_name, function(x) sum(x == 0))
zeros[zeros > 0]
#>   Alaska Nebraska New York    Texas 
#>       40        2       62        3
units <- table(cty$state_name)
names(zeros)[zeros == units[names(zeros)]]
#> [1] "Alaska"   "New York"

There it is. In Alaska and New York, every reporting unit shows zero third-party vote. Those are exactly the two states at the top of our disagreement plot. The data does not say “no one voted third party in New York.” It says the person compiling this file never got New York’s third-party numbers.

A zero and a missing value are not the same thing, and spreadsheets cannot tell them apart. This is the most important sentence in the lab.

Now watch the same disease in the other file. The state file has an other column too:

sum(st$other == 0)
#> [1] 42

42 of 51 states report zero third-party vote. But those three percentages should add to 100. Do they?

st$total_pct <- st$harris + st$trump + st$other
range(st$total_pct)
#> [1] 96.15 99.48
sum(abs(st$total_pct - 100) <= 0.01)
#> [1] 0

Not one state sums to 100. Every state is short by one to four points — and that shortfall is the third-party vote, sitting there unlabelled. We can recover it:

st$other_implied <- round(100 - st$harris - st$trump, 2)
head(st[order(-st$other_implied), c("state", "other", "other_implied")], 5)
#>         state other other_implied
#> 2      Alaska  1.68          4.05
#> 46    Vermont  0.00          3.85
#> 48 Washington  0.00          3.80
#> 38     Oregon  0.00          3.76
#> 21   Maryland  0.00          3.30

So now we can estimate how many ballots the county file never saw. If the county file’s Harris count is right, and the state file’s Harris share is right, then the true statewide total must be the count divided by the share:

cmp$implied_total <- round(cmp$votes_dem / (cmp$harris / 100))
cmp$missing       <- cmp$implied_total - cmp$total_votes
cmp$missing_pct   <- round(100 * cmp$missing / cmp$implied_total, 2)

head(cmp[order(-cmp$missing_pct), c("state_name", "total_votes",
                                    "implied_total", "missing", "missing_pct")], 6)
#>      state_name total_votes implied_total missing missing_pct
#> 2        Alaska      324097        337334   13237        3.92
#> 33     New York     8198094       8380252  182158        2.17
#> 51      Wyoming      266353        269067    2714        1.01
#> 35 North Dakota      365059        368165    3106        0.84
#> 46      Vermont      366389        369405    3016        0.82
#> 21     Maryland     3015650       3038290   22640        0.75

Alaska is missing about 13,000 ballots — 3.9% of everything cast there — and New York roughly 182,000, or 2.2%. Those are not rounding errors. They are entire candidates.

We will test this diagnosis properly in the exercises.

Part 4: Joining on names is a trap

Everything so far compared states, where there are only 51 things and the names are unambiguous. Counties are where joins go to die.

Bring in the Census Bureau’s official county list. This is the first time two families meet in this course: returns assembled by a news organisation, checked against geography defined by a federal agency. Watch which one you end up trusting, and notice that you did not decide it on evidence — you decided it on who produced the file.

head(cen)
#>    fips           name state_abbrev state_name
#> 1 01001 Autauga County           AL    Alabama
#> 2 01003 Baldwin County           AL    Alabama
#> 3 01005 Barbour County           AL    Alabama
#> 4 01007    Bibb County           AL    Alabama
#> 5 01009  Blount County           AL    Alabama
#> 6 01011 Bullock County           AL    Alabama
nrow(cen)
#> [1] 3144

3,144 county-equivalents. Our returns file has 3,160 rows. Close, and we will come back to the gap.

Suppose we want to attach these official records to our returns. The obvious move is to match on the county name. Try it:

by_name <- merge(cty, cen, by.x = "county_name", by.y = "name")
nrow(by_name)
#> [1] 14492

Pause. We put in 3,160 rows of returns and got out more than 14,000. Where did they come from?

merge() matches every row on the left against every row on the right that shares the key. If a name appears in several states, you get every combination:

sort(table(cty$county_name), decreasing = TRUE)[1:6]
#> 
#> Washington County  Jefferson County   Franklin County    Jackson County 
#>                30                25                24                23 
#>    Lincoln County    Madison County 
#>                23                19
c(returns = sum(cty$county_name == "Washington County"),
  census  = sum(cen$name == "Washington County"),
  joined  = sum(by_name$county_name == "Washington County"))
#> returns  census  joined 
#>      30      30     900

Thirty Washington Counties on each side, matched every-which-way: \(30 \times 30 = 900\) rows, of which 30 are right and 870 are garbage. County names are not unique and were never meant to be.

The usual first fix is to match on state and name together. paste() glues strings into one key:

cty$key <- paste(cty$state_name, cty$county_name)
cen$key <- paste(cen$state_name, cen$name)

nrow(merge(cty, cen, by = "key"))
#> [1] 3112

Much better. But we started with 3,160 rows and only 3,112 came through:

missed <- cty[!cty$key %in% cen$key, ]
table(missed$state_name)
#> 
#>               Alaska District of Columbia 
#>                   40                    8

Alaska and the District of Columbia, entirely. Hold that thought.

Part 5: The join that succeeds and is still wrong

Names are bad keys. Codes are what codes are for. Join on FIPS instead:

by_fips <- merge(cty, cen, by.x = "county_fips", by.y = "fips")
nrow(by_fips)
#> [1] 3116

3,116 matched, up from 3,112. Which returns still found no home?

table(cty$state_name[!cty$county_fips %in% cen$fips])
#> 
#>               Alaska District of Columbia 
#>                   37                    7

And which official counties got no returns?

table(cen$state_name[!cen$fips %in% cty$county_fips])
#> 
#> Alaska Hawaii 
#>     27      1

Now here is the part that should make you uneasy. We joined on a code, so whatever matched should be the same place. Check it — compare the name that came from the returns against the name that came from the Census:

wrong <- by_fips[by_fips$county_name != by_fips$name, ]
wrong[, c("county_fips", "state_name.x", "county_name", "name", "total_votes")]
#>     county_fips         state_name.x             county_name
#> 68        02013               Alaska State House District 13
#> 69        02016               Alaska State House District 16
#> 70        02020               Alaska State House District 20
#> 295       11001 District of Columbia                  Ward 1
#>                           name total_votes
#> 68      Aleutians East Borough        7271
#> 69  Aleutians West Census Area        9273
#> 70      Anchorage Municipality        6965
#> 295       District of Columbia       40463

Read that table slowly. Four rows joined successfully to the wrong place. Alaska’s State House District 13 is now labelled Aleutians East Borough. Anchorage Municipality — a city of nearly 300,000 — has been handed 6,965 votes from a state legislative district. And the District of Columbia, all 700,000 residents of it, is now Ward 1.

Nothing errored. Nothing warned. If you had joined and moved on, you would have published it.

Three places that don’t have counties

The four wrong matches and the 44 orphans all come from the same place: three jurisdictions that do not report presidential results by county at all.

Alaska has 30 boroughs and census areas, but does not tabulate votes in them. It reports by state house district — 40 of them. There is no federal code for “Alaska House District 7,” so whoever built this file invented one by tacking the district number onto Alaska’s state code 02. That is a reasonable improvisation right up to the moment it collides with real codes 02013, 02016 and 02020, which belong to actual boroughs.

head(cty[cty$state_name == "Alaska", c("county_fips", "county_name", "total_votes")], 4)
#>    county_fips            county_name total_votes
#> 68       02001 State House District 1        8228
#> 69       02002 State House District 2        9105
#> 70       02003 State House District 3       10626
#> 71       02004 State House District 4        8852
head(cen[cen$state_abbrev == "AK", c("fips", "name")], 4)
#>     fips                       name
#> 68 02013     Aleutians East Borough
#> 69 02016 Aleutians West Census Area
#> 70 02020     Anchorage Municipality
#> 71 02050         Bethel Census Area

The District of Columbia is one county-equivalent, 11001. This file splits it into eight wards and numbers them 11001 through 11008 — so Ward 1 inherits the code that means “all of DC.”

cty[cty$state_name == "District of Columbia",
    c("county_fips", "county_name", "total_votes")]
#>     county_fips county_name total_votes
#> 332       11001      Ward 1       40463
#> 333       11002      Ward 2       37959
#> 334       11003      Ward 3       44584
#> 335       11004      Ward 4       42403
#> 336       11005      Ward 5       45114
#> 337       11006      Ward 6       48678
#> 338       11007      Ward 7       37037
#> 339       11008      Ward 8       29631
cen[cen$state_abbrev == "DC", c("fips", "name")]
#>      fips                 name
#> 322 11001 District of Columbia

Hawaii is the small mystery in the other direction — one official county with no returns:

cen[cen$state_abbrev == "HI", c("fips", "name")]
#>      fips            name
#> 549 15001   Hawaii County
#> 550 15003 Honolulu County
#> 551 15005  Kalawao County
#> 552 15007    Kauai County
#> 553 15009     Maui County
cty[cty$state_name == "Hawaii", c("county_fips", "county_name", "total_votes")]
#>     county_fips     county_name total_votes
#> 566       15001   Hawaii County       82823
#> 567       15003 Honolulu County      340921
#> 568       15007    Kauai County       30064
#> 569       15009     Maui County       62893

Kalawao County has about eighty residents. It is the former leprosy settlement on Molokai, it is administered by the state health department, and its ballots are counted with Maui’s. It is a real county that never appears in election returns.

Part 6: The same source changed its mind

One more failure, and it is the sneakiest. Both county files came from the same repository, built by the same person, four years apart. Surely those can be compared.

c(rows_2020 = nrow(old), rows_2024 = nrow(cty))
#> rows_2020 rows_2024 
#>      3152      3160
sum(!cty$county_fips %in% old$county_fips)   # in 2024, not in 2020
#> [1] 56
sum(!old$county_fips %in% cty$county_fips)   # in 2020, not in 2024
#> [1] 48
table(cty$state_name[!cty$county_fips %in% old$county_fips])
#> 
#>               Alaska          Connecticut District of Columbia 
#>                   40                    9                    7
table(old$state_name[!old$county_fips %in% cty$county_fips])
#> 
#>      Alaska Connecticut 
#>          40           8

Three states, three different stories.

Connecticut abolished its counties. Connecticut’s eight counties stopped functioning as governments in 1960 and survived only as statistical lines on a map. The state eventually asked the Census Bureau to replace them with the nine planning regions its councils of government actually use, and the Bureau agreed in a Federal Register notice dated June 6, 2022. New boundaries, new names, new codes:

old[old$state_name == "Connecticut", c("county_fips", "county_name")]
#>     county_fips       county_name
#> 320       09001  Fairfield County
#> 321       09003   Hartford County
#> 322       09005 Litchfield County
#> 323       09007  Middlesex County
#> 324       09009  New Haven County
#> 325       09011 New London County
#> 326       09013    Tolland County
#> 327       09015    Windham County
cty[cty$state_name == "Connecticut", c("county_fips", "county_name")]
#>     county_fips                                    county_name
#> 320       09110                        Capitol Planning Region
#> 321       09120             Greater Bridgeport Planning Region
#> 322       09130 Lower Connecticut River Valley Planning Region
#> 323       09140               Naugatuck Valley Planning Region
#> 324       09150       Northeastern Connecticut Planning Region
#> 325       09160                Northwest Hills Planning Region
#> 326       09170      South Central Connecticut Planning Region
#> 327       09180       Southeastern Connecticut Planning Region
#> 328       09190            Western Connecticut Planning Region
length(intersect(old$county_fips[old$state_name == "Connecticut"],
                 cty$county_fips[cty$state_name == "Connecticut"]))
#> [1] 0

Zero codes in common. And the regions are not the counties regrouped — the lines themselves moved, so there is no lookup table that turns one into the other without going back to town-level data.

Alaska got renumbered by the compiler. In 2020 this source coded Alaska’s districts 02901–02940, deliberately staying clear of real borough codes. In 2024 it switched to 02001–02040, which does not:

head(old$county_fips[old$state_name == "Alaska"], 3)
#> [1] "02901" "02902" "02903"
head(cty$county_fips[cty$state_name == "Alaska"], 3)
#> [1] "02001" "02002" "02003"

That was not a change in the world. That was a change in one person’s convention, and nothing in the file announces it.

DC changed shape. In 2020 this source had one DC row. In 2024 it has eight.

old[old$state_name == "District of Columbia", c("county_fips", "county_name")]
#>     county_fips          county_name
#> 331       11001 District of Columbia

Now put it together. Suppose you want the swing from 2020 to 2024 in every county. You join on FIPS:

sw <- merge(old[, c("county_fips", "state_name", "county_name",
                    "votes_dem", "votes_gop")],
            cty[, c("county_fips", "votes_dem", "votes_gop")],
            by = "county_fips", suffixes = c("_20", "_24"))
nrow(sw)
#> [1] 3104
sw$r20 <- 100 * sw$votes_gop_20 / (sw$votes_gop_20 + sw$votes_dem_20)
sw$r24 <- 100 * sw$votes_gop_24 / (sw$votes_gop_24 + sw$votes_dem_24)
sw$swing <- round(sw$r24 - sw$r20, 2)

head(sw[order(-sw$swing), c("state_name", "county_name", "r20", "r24", "swing")], 6)
#>      state_name     county_name      r20      r24 swing
#> 2647      Texas Maverick County 45.23105 59.29876 14.07
#> 170  California Imperial County 37.54525 50.43987 12.89
#> 2725      Texas     Webb County 38.24389 51.09587 12.85
#> 1793   New York    Bronx County 16.00987 27.28238 11.27
#> 2699      Texas    Starr County 47.47841 58.02801 10.55
#> 1831   New York   Queens County 27.20535 37.70113 10.50

That is a real and famous result — the biggest Republican shifts of 2024 were in heavily Hispanic border counties in south Texas and in Imperial County, California, with the New York City boroughs close behind.

And then there is this row:

sw[sw$county_fips == "11001",
   c("county_fips", "county_name", "r20", "r24", "swing")]
#>     county_fips          county_name      r20      r24 swing
#> 283       11001 District of Columbia 5.533046 5.280189 -0.25

Look at what that says. All of the District of Columbia in 2020, compared against Ward 1 in 2024, producing a swing of \(-0.25\) points. The number is not absurd. It is not flagged. It sits in a table of 3,104 rows and looks exactly like its neighbours. It is also meaningless.

This is the lesson of the lab. A join that produces plausible output is not a join that is correct. The only way to know is to check the join itself — count your rows, look at what dropped, and look at what matched.

Part 7: On your own

This is the part you turn in. You are not being asked to write code. Each option below is a working chunk with one thing to change, or nothing at all to change. Run it, look at what comes out, and tell me what it means.

Pick one.

Option A — Test the diagnosis

Part 3 blamed the disagreement on the county file’s denominator: it misses third-party ballots, so its Harris share comes out too high. That is a claim about the world, and it makes a prediction we can check. If the counts are fine and only the denominator is wrong, then throwing third parties out of both files should make the disagreement disappear.

# All-party share (what Part 3 compared)
cmp$dh <- round(100 * cmp$votes_dem / cmp$total_votes - cmp$harris, 2)

# Two-party share — third parties removed from both sides
cmp$h2_cty <- 100 * cmp$votes_dem / (cmp$votes_dem + cmp$votes_gop)
cmp$h2_st  <- 100 * cmp$harris    / (cmp$harris    + cmp$trump)
cmp$d2     <- round(cmp$h2_cty - cmp$h2_st, 2)

c(median_gap_all_party = median(abs(cmp$dh)),
  median_gap_two_party = median(abs(cmp$d2)))
#> median_gap_all_party median_gap_two_party 
#>                 0.02                 0.00
c(states_agreeing_all_party = sum(abs(cmp$dh) < 0.05),
  states_agreeing_two_party = sum(abs(cmp$d2) < 0.05))
#> states_agreeing_all_party states_agreeing_two_party 
#>                        30                        49
head(cmp[order(-abs(cmp$d2)), c("state_name", "dh", "d2", "missing_pct")], 5)
#>    state_name   dh    d2 missing_pct
#> 36       Ohio 0.09  0.07        0.20
#> 2      Alaska 1.69 -0.06        3.92
#> 3     Arizona 0.00 -0.01        0.00
#> 48 Washington 0.40  0.01        0.70
#> 1     Alabama 0.13  0.00        0.39

Write about: did the prediction hold? Say what happened to the number of states that agree. Then look at the handful that still disagree — check their missing_pct column. Does the leftover disagreement have the same explanation as the original, or a different one? A diagnosis that survives a test it could have failed is worth more than one that was never tested; say whether this one earned that.

Option B — Rank the states by data quality

Which states’ county returns are least complete?

n <- 12                                  # <- change this number

q <- cmp[order(-cmp$missing_pct), ][1:n, ]
q <- q[order(q$missing_pct), ]

par(mar = c(5, 10, 4, 2))
barplot(q$missing_pct, names.arg = q$state_name, horiz = TRUE, las = 1,
        col = "#4D4D4D", border = NA,
        xlab = "% of ballots the county file never saw",
        main = "Where the county returns are least complete")

# Is incompleteness about how big a state is?
round(cor(cmp$missing_pct, log(cmp$total_votes)), 3)
#> [1] -0.189

Write about: name the worst states. Then take the correlation seriously — it is about \(-0.19\), which is nearly nothing. So incompleteness is not explained by state size. Try to say what it is explained by, and be willing to end at “these are individual state reporting decisions, not a pattern.” That is a real finding, and it is more honest than inventing a story. Why would it matter to a journalist which states these are?

Option C — Where did the country move, and who is missing?

The famous 2024 result — big Republican swings along the Texas border and in the Bronx — with the question the headline never asks.

top_sw <- head(sw[order(-sw$swing), ], 10)
top_sw <- top_sw[order(top_sw$swing), ]

par(mar = c(5, 12, 4, 2))
barplot(top_sw$swing, names.arg = paste0(top_sw$county_name, ", ",
        substr(top_sw$state_name, 1, 2)), horiz = TRUE, las = 1,
        col = "#B2182B", border = NA,
        xlab = "Republican two-party swing, 2020 to 2024 (points)",
        main = "Largest Republican swings")

# Now the bookkeeping the headline skips
c(counties_in_2024_file = nrow(cty),
  counties_in_2020_file = nrow(old),
  counties_that_matched = nrow(sw))
#> counties_in_2024_file counties_in_2020_file counties_that_matched 
#>                  3160                  3152                  3104
setdiff(cty$state_name, sw$state_name)     # states with no rows at all
#> [1] "Alaska"      "Connecticut"
sw[sw$county_fips == "11001", c("county_name", "r20", "r24", "swing")]
#>              county_name      r20      r24 swing
#> 283 District of Columbia 5.533046 5.280189 -0.25

Write about: describe the pattern in the figure. Then do the part the headline skips — two whole states are missing from this analysis entirely, and one row in the table is comparing two different things. Name them, explain why each happened, and say whether their absence changes how much you would trust a national story built on this table.

Option D — Ask your own question

If something in this lab made you suspicious, chase it. You do not need new code — re-running an existing chunk with a different state, a different year, or a different threshold is enough. A sharp question answered with a chunk you barely touched beats an elaborate figure with nothing to say.

What to submit. Knit this document to HTML or PDF and upload it to Canvas, with your chosen chunk and two or three paragraphs of interpretation.

The writing is the assignment. I am not grading your code — it is my code. I am grading whether you can look at a result and tell me what it does and does not support.

One answer is always available to you and is always worth full marks when it is true: the data cannot support this claim, and here is the check that convinced me.

What today was really about

Four things broke, and it is worth sorting them by cause.

Two were about this family specifically. The missing third-party votes and the county that changed meaning between 2020 and 2024 happen because no single body produces American election returns. Fifty-one jurisdictions certify separately, a scraper stitches them together, and the stitching inherits every inconsistency underneath. A census or an FEC filing cannot fail this way, because somebody is accountable for the whole file.

Two were general. Joining on names rather than codes, and a join that succeeds while still being wrong, will bite you in any dataset in any field. You will meet both again in Week 12 with census geography.

So the lesson is not “election data is bad.” It is that each family fails in its own characteristic way, and knowing the family tells you what to check first:

  • Returns — who assembled this, from how many separate sources, and does it match the certified count? (Ours was about 8,000 votes off for one candidate.)
  • The census — what exactly was counted, on what date, and what is the margin of error? (Week 2)
  • Surveys — who was asked, how many refused, and how were the rest weighted? (Week 3)
  • Administrative records — what was this collected for, and what does that purpose leave out? (Weeks 5 and 7)

Those four questions are most of what this course teaches. Everything after today is practice.

Where the data came from

County returns, 2020 and 2024 — Tony McGovern, United States General Election Presidential Results by District, Ward, or County from 2008 to 2024 (https://github.com/tonmcg/US_County_Level_Election_Results_08-24, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14223604). The repository’s README is worth reading precisely because it is candid: the 2024 figures were scraped from Fox News’s results pages, the 2020 figures from Fox News, Politico and the New York Times, and the README states plainly that the results “are not authoritative.” Almost every county-level analysis you will read in the press rests on a file like this one. Its national totals land about 8,000 votes below the certified count for Trump and 11,000 below for Harris — impressively close, and still not the official number.

Official county list — U.S. Census Bureau, 2024 Gazetteer Files, Counties (https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/gazetteer/2024_Gazetteer/), trimmed to codes and names for the 50 states and DC. This is the legal geography: what officially counts as a county in 2024.

State returns — the identical file you used in Week 1, built from jaytimm’s PresElectionResults compilation. Its vote columns are percentages, and its other column is zero wherever the source did not separately tabulate third-party votes — which, as Part 3 showed, is most of the country.

The script that downloaded, trimmed and checked all of this is data/build-data.R. Run it and it will rebuild every file in the folder from the original sources. You should be able to ask that of any dataset you are handed, and you should be suspicious when you cannot.
